result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.transform_with_spanner()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Transform graph to a spanner with given stretch. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L12844-L12996){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.transform_with_spanner(stretch, weight=None, seed=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} A spanner is a sparse subgraph that approximates distances in the original graph. For any pair of nodes `u` and `v`, the distance in the spanner is at most `stretch=` times the distance in the original graph: `distance_spanner(u, v) ≤ stretch × distance_original(u, v)` The resulting spanner preserves approximate distances while using fewer edges, making it useful for graph compression, network backbone extraction, and approximate distance queries. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [stretch]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Maximum distance approximation factor. Must be ≥ `1.0`. Lower `stretch=` values give better approximations but more edges. Higher `stretch=` values create sparser spanners. [weight]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edge attribute to use as distance/weight. If `None`, all edges have weight `1` (unweighted graph). [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for reproducibility. The algorithm has randomized components, so different seeds may produce different spanners with the same stretch guarantee. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with the same nodes but a subset of edges that forms a spanner with the specified stretch. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If stretch < `1.0` or if graph is directed. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} **Algorithm**: This implements a greedy spanner algorithm that iteratively adds edges if they improve the stretch bound. The Baswana-Sen randomized algorithm [1]_ would provide better theoretical guarantees but is more complex. **Complexity**: O(mn) where m = number of edges, n = number of nodes. For sparse graphs this is O(n²), for dense graphs O(n³). **Sparsity**: The number of edges in the spanner depends on the stretch: - unweighted graphs: `O(n^(1+1/k))` edges where `k = ⌊(stretch+1)/2⌋` - weighted graphs: May have more edges but still significantly fewer than the original graph **Properties**: - preserves graph connectivity - guarantees stretch bound for all node pairs - returns undirected graph (same as input) - preserves node attributes - preserves edge weights (when `weight` parameter is provided) **Use Cases**: - network backbones: extract core network structure - graph compression: reduce storage while preserving distances - approximate queries: fast distance estimation - visualization: simplify dense networks for clearer plots - preprocessing: reduce graph size before expensive algorithms ## Examples {.doc-examples} Create a simple 2-spanner (distances at most 2× original): ::: {#68ae4cd3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph() for i in range(5): g.add_node(label=str(i)) # Create a cycle for i in range(5): g.add_edge(source=str(i), target=str((i+1) % 5)) spanner = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=2.0) # Returns True: Fewer edges spanner.count_edges() < g.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Create a 3-spanner of a weighted graph: ::: {#0b20fdef .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph(weighted=True) g.add_node(label="A") g.add_node(label="B") g.add_node(label="C") g.add_edge(source="A", target="B", weight=1.0) g.add_edge(source="B", target="C", weight=1.0) g.add_edge(source="A", target="C", weight=5.0) spanner = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=3.0, weight="weight") # The direct A-C edge might be omitted since going A->B->C # gives distance 2, which is < 3 × (distance 5) # Returns True spanner.count_edges() <= 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Compare sparsity for different stretch values: ::: {#de66cba8 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import networkx as nx # Create a random graph nx_g = nx.erdos_renyi_graph(50, 0.1, seed=23) g = ec.Graph() for node in nx_g.nodes(): g.add_node(label=str(node)) for u, v in nx_g.edges(): g.add_edge(source=str(u), target=str(v)) original_edges = g.count_edges() spanner2 = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=2.0, seed=23) spanner3 = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=3.0, seed=23) # Higher stretch -> fewer edges result = spanner3.count_edges() < spanner2.count_edges() < original_edges # Returns True result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Extract network backbone for visualization: ::: {#18cde9ef .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ec.Graph() # ... build large social network ... # Extract 2-spanner for cleaner visualization backbone = g.transform_with_spanner(stretch=2.0) # Now visualize backbone instead of full graph ``` :::
